structured_data_json_ld.description: Practical tips and advice about what to do if you're struggling with a low mood, sadness or depression.

hasPart.description: Most people feel low sometimes, but if it's affecting your life, there are things you can try to help. Support is also available.

hasPart.text: Signs of a low mood include feeling sad, anxious and more tired than usual. A low mood that lasts more than 2 weeks could be depression.
If you have a low mood, it can help to talk to other people, take regular exercise and try to avoid focusing on things you cannot change.
You may need medical help if your low mood does not go away and nothing you are trying seems to help.

hasPart.description: Signs of a low mood include feeling sad, anxious and more tired than usual. A low mood that lasts more than 2 weeks could be depression.

hasPart.text:
A general low mood can make you feel sad, anxious or panicky, angry or frustrated and low on confidence and self-esteem. It can also make you feel tired, or cause problems sleeping.

A low mood often gets better after a few days or weeks.

It's usually possible to improve a low mood by making small changes in your life. For example, resolving something that's bothering you or getting more sleep.

Symptoms of depression

If you have a low mood that lasts 2 weeks or more, it could be a sign of depression.

Other symptoms of depression may include:

  • not getting any enjoyment out of life
  • feeling hopeless
  • not being able to concentrate on everyday things
  • having suicidal thoughts or thoughts about harming yourself

hasPart.headline: Signs of a low mood

hasPart.description: If you have a low mood, it can help to talk to other people, take regular exercise and try to avoid focusing on things you cannot change.

hasPart.headline: Do
hasPart.text:
• try talking about your feelings to a friend, family member, healthcare professional or counsellor

  • consider peer support, where people use their experiences to help each other

  • get regular exercise – this may improve your mood and help you sleep better

  • eat a healthy diet with regular meals to keep your energy levels stable

  • try mindfulness techniques, where you focus on the present moment

hasPart.headline: Don't
hasPart.text:
• do not try to do everything at once – set small targets that you can easily achieve

  • do not focus on the things you cannot change – focus your time and energy on helping yourself feel better

  • try not to tell yourself that you're alone – most people feel low sometimes and support is available

  • try not to use alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to relieve a low mood – these can all contribute to poor mental health

hasPart.description: You may need medical help if your low mood does not go away and nothing you are trying seems to help.

hasPart.text: If your low mood does not go away and the things you’re doing are not helping, then you may need medical help.

hasPart.text:

  • you're struggling to cope with a low mood
  • things you're trying yourself are not helping

Things you can try to help with a low mood
Do
try talking about your feelings to a friend, family member, healthcare professional or counsellor
consider peer support, where people use their experiences to help each other
get regular exercise – this may improve your mood and help you sleep better
eat a healthy diet with regular meals to keep your energy levels stable
try mindfulness techniques, where you focus on the present moment
Don’t
do not try to do everything at once – set small targets that you can easily achieve
do not focus on the things you cannot change – focus your time and energy on helping yourself feel better
try not to tell yourself that you're alone – most people feel low sometimes and support is available
try not to use alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to relieve a low mood – these can all contribute to poor mental health

sections.heading: Causes of a low mood
sections.text:
Causes of a low mood
There are many reasons why you might feel low at some point in your life.
Any sort of difficult event or experience could lead to sadness or low self-esteem. Sometimes it's possible to feel low without there being an obvious reason.
Identifying the cause
If you know what's causing your low mood it might be easier to find ways to manage it.
Some examples of things that may cause a low mood include:
work – feeling pressure at work, unemployment or retirement
family – relationship difficulties, divorce or
caring for someone
financial problems – unexpected bills or borrowing money
health – illness or injury
bereavement
(losing someone or something)
Even significant life events, such as buying a house, having a baby or planning a wedding, could lead to feelings of sadness.
You might find it hard to explain to people why you feel this way, but talking to someone could help you find a solution.
